title: Larne & Kilwaughter
standfirst: East Antrim records preserve several Glasgow households from 1653 onward. One later father-and-son link is explicit; the connections between the older households, and to collateral Irish lines, are still questions. An inspected 1821 Crossle abstract now names a later Larne sibling household; its links to named profiles remain possible comparisons.
question: Can the seventeenth-century Larne, Glenarm and Kilwaughter occurrences be connected to the later documented Kilwaughter family without filling the missing generations by name or locality alone?
answer: The 20 December1764 Ballykeel lease proves that James Glasgow was Robert Glasgow’s son. It does not name Robert’s father or supply the missing earlier generations. The local working tree now tentatively connects Robert of Larne through a possible1618 Glasgow identity and places the Belfast shipmaster James beneath him. These selected uncertain links supply a provisional shared family, not documentary proof; the later Larne and Inishrush identity comparisons remain separate questions. The working model now places Adam of Inishrush and the reconstructed older Alexander under the older Larne ropemaker, both uncertain; it does not prove either son or James’s own ancestry. The inspected 1821 Crossle census abstract independently records Ann Glasgow, 50, with sister Jane and brother James, both 47, at No. 22 Main Street, Larne. This strengthens the possible comparison between that Ann/Jane pair and the 1832 lease renewal, while Ann-3992 and James-3986 remain unproved identities. It does not change any earlier parent or sibling attachment.

chapters.title: Ann, Jane and James at No. 22 Main Street
body: Research rationale, 23 October 2026: test whether an independently recorded Larne household helps identify the Anne and Jane Glasgow named together in the 25 February 1832 renewal of James Glasgow’s 1779 Newtown lease. The inspected Crossle genealogical abstract, page 23, image 00142, is headed 1821 census, County Antrim, parish and town of Larne. At No. 22 Main Street it records Ann Glasgow, 50, Jane, her sister, 47, and James, her brother, 47. The sibling roles are explicit for these record subjects. The ages imply births about 1770–1771 for Ann and 1773–1774 for Jane and James; these are estimates, not recorded birth dates. Equal reported ages do not establish twins. This is an abstract of the census, not an inspection of the original census sheet; uncertain occupation and land-note readings are not used.

The 1832 lease renewal names Anne and Jane Glasgow. The 1821 Ann/Jane sibling household supplies a specific, independently recorded pair in Larne and strengthens a possible identity across the records. No inspected record equates No. 22 Main Street with the recital’s 24-foot north-side tenement or proves that the same women held it in 1832. Ann Glasgow-3992, monument-defined daughter of James Glasgow-3991 and his wife Jane, remains a possible identification for the abstract’s Ann. Her monument-derived birth about 1767–1768 differs by roughly three years from the abstract age; that discrepancy does not decide the identity. The monument father died in 1812 and his wife Jane died in 1820, so neither can be the living 1821 brother James or sister Jane. Their documented parentage stays confined to the monument-defined Ann; no parentage transfers to the abstract household.

James Glasgow-3986, with an uncertain birth about 1773 and a Larne association, is a compatible comparison for the 47-year-old brother only. His adult identity, possible 1830 freehold application and proposed father James-1509 remain separately uncertain. Shared sibling surnames support a natal-Glasgow reading but do not independently prove birth surnames or parents. The current study selects no existing-profile sibling edge, parent, identity merge or vital correction from the abstract. Earlier Larne ropemaker, estate and parent-confidence assessments retain their separate grades. The 1832 renewal and intervening title records, the exact premises, and a named parent or sibling bridge are the next discriminators.

chapters.title: James the ropemaker: Hugh preferred as father, possible 52%
body: Research rationale: choose the strongest existing parent hypothesis for a substantial Larne/Inishrush branch rather than leaving the recorded Hugh comparison outside the working family.

Select Hugh Glasgow-1499 as the preferred possible father of James Glasgow-1509, the older Belfast/Larne ropemaker, at 52% subjective confidence, replacing William Glasgow-1505 in the local working tree. The archived chronology explicitly places a James, son of Hugh, at New Town/Larne in 1737 and identifies its reported 1762 Janet Shutter groom with that James. Hugh is an independently documented Larne merchant and elder, jointly leasing Newtown property in1736 and dealing with Hugh Shutter in the original1749 mortgage. The later James/Janet account and the distinctive Jane Shutter name in the younger William’s monument fit a recurring Glasgow–Shutter network. These combined named-parent, locality, generation and family-association clues favour Hugh over retaining a William father without a named-son record.

This is a preferred working identification, not a proved father clause for the adult ropemaker. The chronology is one derivative reconstruction: its1737 child,1762 groom and reported1737–1802 stone must not be counted as three independent confirmations. The adult’s1737 birth may itself derive from that reconstruction; the independent1773 affidavit establishes only birth before27 October1743. The original1737 entry,1762 marriage and alleged James/Janet stone remain uninspected. Hugh Shutter’s relationship to Janet is unknown, and a business association does not identify a father-in-law. A different Hugh remains possible. No mother is selected: Ann is not established as the1737 child’s mother by the reviewed account.

The monument’s separately recorded James Glasgow-3991, son of Hugh and Ann, died in1812 aged64 and belongs to the younger1747/48 generation. That is a serious rival explanation: the reported1737 child could have died and the name been used again. It is not a recorded death of that earlier child. Withdraw the categorical earlier inference that the1737 James must have died young. Do not equate the two James profiles, invent a second wife, or infer surviving brothers with the same forename as an established fact. The older ropemaker was already an adult in1760–1761 and over thirty in1773, so he remains distinct from the younger monument/tanner comparison.

Retain William Glasgow-1505 as an unselected uncertain father alternative at27%, preserving his earlier possible but individually unrated placement. A William Glasgow, Larne merchant, witnessed the1760 ropewalk lease, which is genuine positive association with James; the witness is not expressly called his father and may be the older William or another adult namesake. William and Hugh’s joint1736/1757 property activity makes a wider family or business relationship plausible without choosing its degree. William could be father, uncle or another associate. The specific reported Hugh-son identification and Hugh–Shutter connection now favour Hugh, but do not exclude William. The percentages express comparative research judgment, not a measured frequency or independent-source calculation.

One selected father is replaced locally. The child-side working branch contains49 retained pre-1850 profile accounts, including James and uncertain descendants; their own grades are unchanged. This is not49 new or proved relationships. The men were already in the same working component, so no component merger or new genealogical connection is claimed. No vital date, place, spouse, mother, identity merge or live WikiTree field changes. Hugh’s own uncertain ancestry and James’s Inishrush descendants retain their prior assessments.

The next discriminators are the original1737 entry,1762 marriage, full James/Janet monument and any surviving1737-child death or later household recital. The1760 William witness must be identified separately rather than silently assigned to the older William. A document naming a parent, sibling or inherited holding would test the preferred model; its absence is not an automatic exclusion.

chapters.title: Kilwaughter: James’s 1669–1726 continuity is probable
body: The preferred identification is one James Glasgow from the Kilwaughter Demesne hearth household of 1669 to the Kilwaughter overseer of probably 29 May 1701 and the later elder marked deceased in 1726. Assess that continuity as probable rather than unresolved. The hearth roll places Jo and James Glascho consecutively in the same demesne, records 5347–5348. The later congregational extracts again contain both names acting for Kilwaughter: John senior in 1700 and an unmarked John in 1700/01, whose individual identity remains open, and James as overseer in probably 1701. John’s already-probable continuity supplies a coherent parallel ageing household, rather than leaving James’s later occurrence as an isolated name match. James’s later elder, 1722 commissioner and 1727 Kilwater probate-index accounts were already assessed as probably one man. The repeated local pairing, the particular district served and an ordinary adult generation in 1700/01 together favour continuity over an otherwise unattested replacement James. The preference uses the combined local sequence; no literal same-man clause is required.

The inference is not documented identity. The later men never occur together in the same reviewed minute, the 1669 roll does not state a kin relationship, and similar spellings are not independent identifiers. Kilwaughter Demesne and the later Kilwaughter district are compatible but not identical address statements. A father-and-son succession or another local James remains possible. Assuming an adult aged at least 21 in 1669 would make James at least about 74 in 1722 and 78 in 1726; those are conditional age calculations, not recorded ages or a new birth bound. His local commission in 1722 is compatible with advanced age, but the long career is the strongest reason for caution. No age at death, occupation, holding or named relative equates the occurrences. The missing 1701–1721 session sequence leaves a real gap. Porter’s 1699–1701 extracts are a printed transcription of a manuscript copy; the later extracts and lost probate index do not independently prove the earlier identity. The probable grade is an overall inference across the groups, not the product of independent probabilities. Neither the 1726 death annotation nor the 1727 probate is newly assigned to a separate earlier James; they remain events of the later elder whose identification with the 1669 man is now probable.

This strengthens the identity at the head of James’s existing 104-profile pre-1850 working branch. The number describes retained profile accounts, including uncertain descendants and unresolved identities. John’s 1669-to-1700 identity was already probable and is not counted as a new upgrade. Exact kinship between John and James remains possible: brother, father and son, uncle and nephew or cousin are not distinguished. Glasgow-3970 of Larne remains their uncertain proposed father. The Scottish Robert and James comparisons, the later South Side family represented by Glasgow-1502 and all mothers retain their separate assessments. No father or mother is regraded, no profile is merged, and no birth, death or place field is changed. Working, supported and confidently marked paternal connectivity are unchanged. This is a re-evaluation of the maintained source readings, not a newly found record or fresh original inspection. Nothing is saved to live WikiTree.

chapters.title: Larne and Inishrush: James’s possible sons Adam and Alexander
body: Glasgow-1509, the older Larne ropemaker, is selected as the uncertain working father of Adam of Inishrush (Glasgow-3902). This adopts the named-family comparison already tested in September. Adam’s gravestone age implies birth about 1758; James’s reported 1737 birth would give an ordinary age-21 generation. The original 1773 affidavit independently places the Larne James’s birth before October 1743, although it does not prove the reported 1737 year. Adam’s proved son James (Glasgow-3903) supplies limited positive naming support. James is a documented adult with a trade and property trail, making him a more useful provisional father than the recordless [Glasgow-3905](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-3905) placeholder. No record names Adam as his child, and the naming argument is weak rather than corroboration of a parent clause.

The same James is selected, with very low confidence, as father of the reconstructed older Alexander (Glasgow-3904). This adopts the existing possible-brother route for Adam and Alexander. On the reported 1737 and estimated 1770 years, James would be about 33 at Alexander’s birth. Making Adam, born about 1758, Alexander’s father instead produces a twelve-year interval. Alexander’s circa 1770 birth is only an estimate, so that calculation does not exclude an Adam father: Alexander could have been born later. However, fatherhood of Daniel by about 1795/96 places Alexander in a generation born by roughly 1775–1778, leaving two short successive generations in the Adam-to-Alexander model. Adam’s wife Unknown-760890, born about 1766/67 from her monument age, cannot be Alexander’s mother on that chronology. The sibling route is therefore preferred provisionally without inventing an earlier wife. Chronological economy does not prove brotherhood or a shared father; neither selected edge is independent support for the other.

A 1760 lease identifies James as a Belfast ropemaker taking a ropewalk at Gardenmore, Larne; the 1768 assignment identifies the same property. This is a real occupational and locality sequence, distinct from the contemporary Larne tanner. Adam is documented much later at Inishrush, and the monument does not state his birthplace. The estimated Inishrush birth cannot exclude a family from elsewhere, but no Belfast birth or Larne-to-Inishrush migration is newly assigned. The 1773 Larne gentleman’s age excludes the younger Glasgow-3991 account; the identity assessment and separation of the two trades retain their previous grades. The reported James/Shutter-46 marriage in 1762 is later than Adam’s birth. It cannot establish Shutter-46 as Adam’s mother. An earlier union, premarital birth or inaccurate reported date would be needed if this father model is right; no such event or person is invented. Shutter-46 is not selected as older Alexander’s mother either: the marriage report and the son identity are independently unproved.

The two local 1740 Tamlaght Hugh households, including Glasgow-3931, and the older Adam-and-Maria naming model remain alternatives for Adam. A different unrecorded father remains possible. Neither Larne property succession nor the Inishrush household totals connect these generations. The 1831 return does not identify its unnamed occupants, and the later plot-29 succession is not evidence of James the ropemaker’s paternity. The shared [Glasgow-3905](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-3905) field is a recently created research placeholder, not evidence that Adam, older Alexander and Glasgow-1367 were brothers. It is not identified or merged with James. No father is extended to Glasgow-1367, and no unnamed extra generation is added.

Older Alexander is himself reconstructed chiefly from late descendant testimony naming Thomas’s parents as Alexander and Rosanna. The 2007 account and its copied 2020 restatement are one source tradition, not independent witnesses. Daniel and Thomas are proved brothers, but their father’s name is not established by a contemporary parent record. The new James father therefore depends on that reconstructed older Alexander account. Younger Glasgow-951 remains a separate, unresolved possible brother or cousin of Thomas and Daniel; the record-defined John Glasgow, farmer (Glasgow-4090), is his selected father, a confident inference at 90% since 23 October 2026. This batch does not select older Alexander as younger Alexander’s father or place that younger family beneath James. No Rosanna surname or October 1822 death date is newly established. James’s own Glasgow-1505 and Glasgow-1499 ancestry alternatives and existing children retain their earlier assessments.

Two named father hypotheses are selected from existing research, with low/very low confidence. No new original inspection, certain relationship upgrade, identity merge or live WikiTree save. All existing vital fields and confidently marked metrics remain unchanged. Mothers are independently unassigned. The local model replaces the placeholder father only in these two selected views; captured WikiTree fields and rival parentage remain available. Counts describe retained profile accounts and conditional ancestry, not a proved pedigree.

chapters.title: The 1652 Edinburgh cordiner: a working Glasgow childhood
body: Select Robert Glasgow-1027 as the uncertain working father of the Edinburgh cordiner Robert Glasgow-3938 through possible identity with the indexed Glasgow child Robert Glasgow-1078, baptised on 17 November 1618. The published Edinburgh marriage register names Robert as a cordiner with Janet Thomsone on 1 July 1652. The older Robert is the probable identity of the Glasgow cordiner admitted burgess on 22 April 1613 and is the named father of the 1618 child. If baptised near birth, that child would have been about 33 at the July 1652 marriage. The matching name, compatible adult generation and same craft make this a useful preferred family comparison over an otherwise unidentified parent or a more distant cordiner kinsman. The trade association supplies a reason to select the family, but neither hereditary training nor a Glasgow-to-Edinburgh move is documented. The father selection is low confidence; it does not identify the child with the adult as an established fact.

Select Jonet Cunningham-20923 as the independently assessed uncertain mother of the Edinburgh adult only through the same possible childhood identity. The 1618 baptism explicitly names Jonet Conynghame as mother of Robert Glasgow-1078. This is an explicit maternal clause for the child, not an inference from the older Robert’s marriage alone or from a Cunningham surname elsewhere. Its transfer to Glasgow-3938 depends entirely on the uncertain identity and therefore remains uncertain. The father’s craft provides no independent evidence of maternity.

Keep Robert Glasgow-1078, Glasgow-3938 and the Larne Robert Glasgow-3970 as separate profile accounts. Both adult accounts are now provisionally placed in the 1618 child’s family; this does not establish two distinct sons named Robert. The 1652 Edinburgh event and the 1653 Larne account are not simultaneous incompatible events on the available evidence: they could concern one mobile man or different namesakes. Neither a migration nor that combined identity is selected as proved. Robert Glasgow-1149 remains the separate existing candidate for the Euphame Lorimer household. Her indexed children in 1651, 1659, 1662 and 1664 bracket the Thomsone marriage, favouring two Edinburgh men. The reported 1 March 1644 West Port sasine also names Eupham Lorimer and belongs to that household comparison; it does not give a West Port residence or wife to the 1652 bridegroom. The original sasine is uninspected. The 1618 child’s attached younger Cunningham spouse and 1645 James association do not prove his adult identity. A later Thomsone marriage could be a remarriage if that association is correct, but no death or remarriage sequence is supplied. Preserve the existing attachments and all namesake alternatives. Glasgow-3938’s before-1634 birth boundary is an age-derived profile estimate, not a recorded birth. It remains unchanged, as do the child’s baptism, the Larne estimate and all existing spouses, children and confidently marked links. The Edinburgh marriage gives no parents, age or children. No apprentice, burgess, witness, property or migration record joins these accounts. An unrelated cordiner or another son, nephew or cousin in the wider family remains possible. No identity merge, new original inspection, live WikiTree save or relationship-confidence upgrade is claimed. Connectivity counts the retained profile accounts, including possible duplicates.

chapters.title: The current provisional Glasgow–Larne–Belfast route
body: Select Robert Glasgow-1027 and Jonet Cunningham-20923 as the uncertain working father and mother of Robert Glaskow of Larne, Glasgow-3970, through the existing possible identity with their son Robert Glasgow-1078, baptised at Glasgow on 17 November 1618. The 1653 Larne account gives no age or parents, and its before-1625 birth boundary permits the 1618 child; that child would have been about 23 during the alleged 1641 events and 35 in 1653. The Scottish child has no established later fate that excludes this adult account. Choose the already recorded possible identity as the working family explanation, at low confidence. The baptism names both parents, so the maternal selection is assessed from that same explicit child clause, not from a Cunningham surname association in Ulster. Both adult parent links depend on the uncertain identity and remain uncertain; the baptism’s direct parentage must not be transferred as proof of the Larne man’s origins.

Select Robert of Larne-3970 as Captain James Glasgow-3172’s uncertain working father. This adopts the existing possible son-or-younger-relative comparison: Larne, Belfast and Kilwaughter form the north-east Antrim setting of the recorded Robert and later James, and an older Robert active in 1641–1653 can precede a shipmaster active by 1667. James commanded the Blessing of Saltcoats in the 1667 Macartney correspondence and the James of Belfast in 1679. These are compatible Scottish-west-coast/Antrim associations, not a parent clause. Son is selected over the unresolved younger-relative alternatives for one provisional paternal route; no mother is selected for James.

Robert-1078 and Robert-3970 remain separate profile accounts of a possible single man; the selected parents do not establish two distinct Robert sons or an identity merge. No record joins the 1618 baptism to Larne, supplies the Larne man’s Scottish origin, or rules out another Robert. The 1666 John of Portrush shipmaster is a further possible identity, not an occupation proved for either Robert; the later Robert/Rachel household remains separate. James-3172, the Scottish child James-3971 of 1645, and the Kilwaughter James-1081 may be one, two or three men. All accounts remain; no identity among those James groups is selected. A child baptised in 1645 could have been a shipmaster aged about 22 in 1667, assuming infant baptism, but that is compatibility only. The father named in that 1645 record is not independently identified with the 1618 child. John-3913’s circa-1630 and Captain James’s circa-1640 births are inherited estimates, not dates that establish or exclude a generation. If John’s 1630 were literal and the Larne man were born in 1618, fatherhood at about twelve would be an important chronological objection; both the age estimate and John’s uncertain paternal attachment require testing. No birth year is changed to force the selected route. Captain James could instead be a nephew, other relative, unrelated namesake, or a member of the Saltcoats sailor John-4152’s family; the named Saltcoats vessel makes that a real competing route, not evidence that John was his father. The two women Cunningham-20923 and Cunningham-22604 are distinct: the elder is the named 1618 mother, the younger the named mother in the 1645 James record. Neither that younger maternity nor a marriage to her is transferred to the Larne adult or captain through these selections. The existing uncertain Kilwaughter father links remain uncertain; none becomes proved by joining their supposed ancestor to Scotland. The Larne allegations are hearsay, not a judicial finding of guilt, and the 1686 will reference is not a proved death date. No new original inspection, certainty upgrade, live WikiTree edit or identity merge is claimed. Connectivity counts profile accounts and does not resolve the possible duplicates.

chapters.title: Separate early occurrences
body: A 1653 deposition places Robert Glaskow at Larne. The 1669 hearth-money roll records Elizabeth at Glenarm and James and John at Kilwaughter.
These are documented local occurrences, not a proved founding family or a line of descent.

evidence.label: Larne evidence synthesis

chapters.title: Three heads of household and a session elder
body: Classon Porter’s printed extracts from the Larne session record name John Glasgow, sen., as stipend bondsman for Kilwaughter and Robert Glasgow for the South Side on 17 May 1700, and James Glasgow as overseer for Kilwaughter, probably on 29 May 1701. The extracts are printed under 1699 and 1700; the weekdays written into the minutes fix the years. They come from a manuscript copy of the session record, not the original.

No Glasgow is among the twenty elders listed from Mr Ogilvie’s ordination in November 1700. James Glasgow stands on the session list that opens the 1721 book, was a commissioner when the Presbytery met at Larne in 1722 and is marked “deceased 1726”; a will of James Glasgow of Kilwater is indexed in 1727. Those four are probably one man. The maintained review now favours, at probable rather than proved strength, identification with the James of the 1669 hearth-money roll; a same-name successor remains possible.

No record states how these men were related to each other, to the 1669 householders or to the men born about 1700–1710. That John and James of 1669 were close kin is possible, on consecutive entries with the same uncommon spelling; brother is no better supported than any other degree. In the printed General Synod rolls no Glasgow represented Larne in any year from 1694 to 1720; the ruling elder James Glasgow of 1698, 1703 and 1705 sat beside the ministers of Drumaul and Duneane.

chapters.title: Larne property, but not kinship
body: A 1736 Newtown lease names William and Hugh Glasgow as joint lessees, and a 1757 deed independently refers to their head lease. Neither document states that they were related.
The 1749 mortgage and later assignments add business and occupational occurrences, not parentage.

chapters.title: A documented Kilwaughter father and son
body: The register chronology and later equity material reconstruct Robert Glasgow and Rachel Wilson’s household at Kilwaughter. The lease of 13 February 1738/9 associates Robert, Rachel and James junior, but does not call James a son; “junior” points to an older namesake and states no relationship.
The original 1764 Ballykeel lease does: its continuation calls him “Jas Glasgow son of the sd Robt”.

body: The Larne monument explicitly names James Glasgow as a son of elder Hugh. The 1843 marriage settlement names property of a deceased Hugh Glasgow, but does not call that Hugh Mary’s father.
The current James–Hugh–Mary chain is a low-confidence working hypothesis. Mary may instead be William’s monument-recorded daughter, whose 1844 death conflicts with the candidate 1843 death.

chapters.title: Mill auction in Larne, Kilwaughter and Inver
body: A 10 September 1804 Caledonian Mercury advertisement announced a 22 September auction at Belfast’s Donegall Arms for Larne corn and wheat mills, Kilwaughter corn mill and Inver flour mills. It names James Holmes & Co. in possession, with separate lease interests under the heirs of the Marquis of Antrim and under the Marquis of Donegall.
This is place-study context only. The passage names no Glasgow surname and does not show that the 1669 Glasgow occurrences operated the mills or glassworks.

clusters.summary: The maintained evidence strongly supports the couple and four named sons, including Archibald.
clusters.boundary: Their American branch does not prove the ancestry of the older Larne households.

clusters.title: James, Hugh and the 1843 bride Mary
clusters.summary: The monument documents James as elder Hugh’s son; the settlement documents a deceased Hugh’s estate connection with Mary.
clusters.boundary: No inspected record states James was the later Hugh’s father or Hugh was Mary’s father. Mary may be William’s daughter, and the 1843/1844 death-year conflict is unresolved.

clusters.title: Tennessee Robert and James J
clusters.summary: Robert’s South Carolina birth and household ages make him a worthwhile candidate for Archibald’s unaccounted-for son, and for James J’s father.
clusters.boundary: Robert→Archibald remains possible 51%. The newly read 1810 original has no male 10–25 tally and cannot track the unnamed 1800 boy. An adult son could have left home. No record yet names Archibald as Robert’s father or Robert as James J’s father; estate 647 is the next named-heir test.

clusters.title: James, ropemaker, of Larne
clusters.summary: The ropemaker has a real adult and property trail; he is a candidate for an older generation in the Inishrush comparison.
clusters.boundary: No record joins him to Adam of Inishrush, and the 1762 marriage leaves Adam’s mother unresolved if this were a father–son link.

clusters.title: Adam of Inishrush
clusters.summary: Adam’s family is a meaningful collateral comparison because the ages can fit a Larne father hypothesis.
clusters.boundary: No document names Adam’s father or joins him to Larne; alternative local origins remain open. Adam, born 1757/8, is too young to be the father of John Glasgow, farmer, if Samuel (born about 1790) was John farmer’s son, so this comparison does not by itself connect the Lisnagaver family.
